newsitem.title: USA: Zinc concs mating partners eye latest spot deal.
newsitem.headline: Zinc concs mating partners eye latest spot deal.

text.p: Zinc miners and smelters, gearing up for their quaintly named mating-season, were taking a close look at the latest and possibly last major spot deal before next year's contract benchmark price is set.
About a week ago Centromin of Peru sold 20,000 tonnes of concentrates to traders for a treatment charge (TC) of just below $160 per tonne, cif Antwerp, officials close to the deal confirmed.
Aggressive traders often pay below TC benchmark contract terms, pegged at $190 per tonne for 1996.
But a North American zinc mining official said that if traders were prepared to accept such low TCs, it showed the market was pretty tight.
He expected no major change in the benchmark TC next year.

A European zinc smelter source said no negotiations for 1997 contracts have taken place so far, but the miners are seeking a $10 to $15 per tonne cut in TCs, taking them back to 1995 levels of about $175. Smelters want a $5 to $10 hike, he added.
Both smelters and miners envisaged a $1,000 LME basis price for 1997 contracts, industry sources said.
However, if zinc prices rise next year as some expect, late contracts may have a higher basis price of about $1,100.
Both sides are mulling the International Lead and Zinc Study Group data which forecast 1997 consumption outpacing mined production.
Several small mine have closed such as Bougrine and Leadville, along with cutbacks at Noranda's Brunswick mine.

And on Monday, an explosion at Noranda's Heath Steele mine stopped operations. The company expected some loss of production but no lengthy shutdown, though it was too early to tell, officials at the Canadian company said.
Analyst Claire Hassall of Brook Hunt expected no major change in 1997 TCs. "I think it certainly won't be higher than it was this year, but maybe a bit lower," Hassall said.
"The market for concentrates is fairly balanced at the moment for next year, with maybe a small surplus," Hassall said.

Last year Pasminco of Australia quickly settled with their Japanese smelter customers in October-November, because they are a net buyer of concentrates and TCs were expected to rise, a mining source said.

"They won't be quite so fast this time," the source added. "The market is genuinely tighter than they thought, and if they go out and roll the terms over at $190 and suddenly find they have to buy at a bit lower, it won't be too bright."

There has been some talk that the escalator component in next year's contracts could be increased sharply to shift more of the zinc market price risk from the mines and onto the smelters to encourage metal output cuts if zinc prices fell.
The European smelter official said because higher zinc prices were expected next year, smelters would probably welcome higher escalators, enabling them to earn more money as the zinc price climbed.
But miners would probably seek some trade off and want to extend the higher escalators beyond 1997 to cover against future falls in metal prices.

"The downside risk in the market seems to be limited, so I can imagine the miners would only do this (raise escalators) with guarantees that it would not be only for one year," the smelter official added.
-- Huw Jones, New York Commodities 212-859-1646
